analysis.one_liner: Sets pesticide residue limits on food at levels protecting infants and children and funds tighter residue monitoring.
analysis.headline: Backed by 21 bipartisan cosponsors and two committee hearings, the bill never reached a Senate vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the nation's pesticide residue rules so that legal limits on food are set at levels that protect infants and children, whose eating habits and sensitivities differ from adults'. It directs the EPA, USDA, and Health and Human Services to follow the National Academy of Sciences' recommendations, requires USDA to collect pesticide-use data on major crops, funds more residue testing of domestic and imported food, and promotes pest-control methods that cut pesticide use. It would bar any tolerance above the level adequate to protect public health, while also adding procedural steps before the EPA can cancel a pesticide and preempting state rules stricter than the federal standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and all food consumers, whose legal residue limits would be set using child-specific toxicity testing and risk assessment, backed by better data and more monitoring of domestic and imported food. States and parents would gain a federal floor built on a National Academy of Sciences report on pesticides in children's diets.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the EPA, USDA, and HHS to establish procedures ensuring pesticide tolerances safeguard the health of infants and children, based on the National Research Council report 'Pesticides in the Diets of Infants and Children,' including child-specific food-consumption data, residue surveillance, and toxicity testing.
Bars the EPA from setting a pesticide tolerance higher than the level it determines is adequate to protect public health, and requires consideration of dietary exposure of infants and children.
Deems food adulterated — and therefore illegal to sell — if it bears a pesticide chemical residue that is unsafe.

Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to collect pesticide-use data of statewide or regional significance for major crops and crops of dietary significance, including fruits and vegetables, to support EPA exposure calculations.
Mandates joint EPA-USDA research and dissemination of integrated pest management techniques so producers can reduce or eliminate pesticides posing more than a negligible dietary risk.
Authorizes appropriations for increased monitoring of pesticide residues in imported and domestic food.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers, whose products could face cancellation, tighter tolerances, and new fees to fund the program; farmers, who could lose pesticide tools and bear transition costs; and taxpayers, who fund the new data collection and residue monitoring.

drawbacks.text: Preempts states from enforcing any pesticide residue limit that is not identical to the federal standard for most qualifying pesticides, unless a state wins a federal petition showing compelling local conditions — taking away a route states had to set tougher food-safety rules than Washington's.

Adds procedural hurdles before the EPA can cancel or restrict a pesticide: the action must rest on a validated test or other significant evidence, pass scientific peer review, include advance notice to the registrant, and clear layered comment and hearing stages — slowing removal of hazardous pesticides.

Allows a tolerance to pose more than a negligible dietary risk if the pesticide's unavailability would limit the availability of an adequate, wholesome, and economical food supply and those effects would outweigh the residue risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The child-protection core is real and responds directly to a National Academy of Sciences report on pesticides in children's diets, and it comes with data collection and monitoring behind it. The costs are ordinary and manageable: slower pesticide cancellations and compliance costs passed partly into food prices. The serious trade-off is the preemption title — states could no longer set stricter residue limits for newer pesticides without winning a federal petition — so the bill traded away a source of tougher state-level protection in exchange for a uniform federal standard.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Agriculture Committee held hearings in June and July 1994 but never voted to send the bill to the Senate floor, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. David Pryor introduced the bill on September 21, 1993, joined as original cosponsors by senators including Richard Lugar, Bob Dole, Nancy Kassebaum, and J. Bennett Johnston.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
The committee held hearings on June 29, 1994, and its Subcommittee on Agricultural Research held hearings on July 28, 1994.
The bill gathered 21 cosponsors — 16 Republicans and 5 Democrats — but no further action was taken, and it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and growers kept the older, looser residue system: no child-based tolerances, extra monitoring, or preemption changes took effect under this bill. Consumers got nothing, because the protections existed only on paper.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill, but 16 of its 21 cosponsors were Republicans — including Senate leaders Bob Dole and Nancy Kassebaum — and the record shows no floor vote or opposition vote at any point.

industries.note: The bill would subject their products to child-health-based tolerances, possible cancellation, and fees. But it also gives them procedural protections before the EPA can cancel a pesticide, national uniformity that blocks stricter state rules, and exceptions allowing more-than-negligible risk to preserve the food supply — so its interest in this bill ran against the strongest consumer protections.

Growers would gain federally funded integrated pest management research to reduce pesticide dependence, but could lose access to pesticides judged above the negligible-risk standard and bear transition costs.

National uniformity would give them a single federal residue standard and bar states from enforcing different limits on qualifying residues, simplifying compliance — at the cost of stricter state rules some consumers favor.
